title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
These data come from the NMES1988 dataset in the AER package, which contains 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987 to 1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. The outcome is visits, the number of physician office visits. The analysis uses five predictors, described below. The reference groups are average for self-perceived health, male for gender, and no for private insurance.

Figure 1: Distribution of the number of physician office visits (counts above 40 are not shown)








The outcome, visits, is a count: it takes only whole numbers and cannot be below zero. Across the 4,406 adults, the mean number of visits was 5.77 and the variance was 45.69, which is about 7.9 times the mean. A Poisson model assumes that the variance equals the mean, so this gap points to overdispersion. About 15.5% of people had no visits at all. The distribution has a long right tail, with a maximum of 89 visits, and 25 people (0.6%) had more than 40 visits. These unusually large counts are one reason to expect that a simple Poisson model may not fit well.

A linear model is a poor choice for the number of physician visits. The DHARMa plots show that the simulated residuals from the Gaussian model do not behave as they should: the QQ plot departs from the diagonal,the formal tests in the table above flag deviations, and the residuals against the predicted values show structure instead of a flat, even spread. These departures appear because the model’s assumptions do not match the data. A Gaussian model treats the outcome as continuous, so it can predict a negative number of visits, which is impossible. It also assumes that the variance is the same at every level of the predictors, yet for counts the variance grows with the mean, so people who are expected to visit often are also the most variable. It treats each predictor as adding a fixed number of visits, whereas for counts it is more natural for a predictor to multiply the expected number of visits. Finally, it ignores that the outcome is made up of whole numbers, with a spike at zero and a long right tail.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Interpreting the comparison
Each likelihood-ratio test compares a model with the one before it. Adding the number of chronic conditions to the null model significantly improved fit (χ²(1) = 2175.4, p < .001), which tells us that chronic conditions are associated with the number of physician visits. Adding health, gender, education, and insurance to M1 also significantly improved fit (χ²(5) = 959.9, p < .001), so these predictors together explain additional variation beyond chronic conditions. I selected M2, the full Poisson model, because it had the lowest AIC (36,597.0) and BIC (36,641.7) and because both tests supported adding predictors. This selection is provisional: it assumes that a Poisson model is appropriate, which I check next.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Interpreting the Poisson diagnostics
The DHARMa plots suggest that the Poisson model does not fit these data well. The simulated residuals depart from the diagonal in the QQ plot, and the residuals against the predicted values show structure instead of a flat, even spread. The dispersion ratio was 7.25 (p < .001), which means the observed variance was about that many times larger than the Poisson model expects. The observed number of zeros was 15.03 times the number the model expects (p < .001).
Overdispersion matters because the Poisson model assumes that the variance equals the mean. When the real variance is larger, the model underestimates the uncertainty in its estimates, so the standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the p-values are too small. Predictors can then look more convincing than the data justify.
I should not move straight to a zero-inflated model on the basis of this zero-inflation test alone, because overdispersion by itself produces extra zeros relative to a Poisson. A Poisson model with the same mean has a thinner spread of counts, so it expects fewer zeros than an overdispersed outcome produces. The apparent excess of zeros may therefore disappear once the model allows for extra variance. The sensible order is to address overdispersion first with a negative binomial model, and then test again whether any excess of zeros remains.

The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the Poisson model, χ²(1) = 12,129.1, p < .001. The test has 1 degree of freedom because the NB2 differs from the Poisson by exactly one parameter: the dispersion parameter, which lets the variance exceed the mean. The Poisson is the special case in which that extra variance is zero.
The comparison changes how the Poisson results should be read. Allowing for overdispersion made the standard errors about 2.5 times larger on average than under the Poisson model, which means the Poisson model was overstating how precisely the associations were estimated. None of the predictors changed from significant to non-significant, so the conclusions about the direction of the associations were stable, even though the uncertainty was larger. In other words, the conclusions I would have drawn from the Poisson model were too confident, even where they were not wrong.

The negative binomial model resolved the overdispersion. The dispersion ratio fell from 7.25 under the Poisson model to 1.04 (p = .428), which is close to 1 and not significant. The residual plots also improved: the QQ plot now follows the diagonal closely, although the plot of residuals against predictions still shows some mild curvature in the quantile lines. One problem remains. The ratio of observed to expected zeros fell from 15.03 to 1.1, but it is still significantly different from 1 (p = .008), which means that the NB2 still produces somewhat fewer zeros than were observed. The excess is small, about 10% more zeros than expected, but because the test is significant I examine in the next section whether the zeros need their own model.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Visualize predicted counts








Figure 8: Predicted number of physician visits by number of chronic conditions (negative binomial model)





The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors. This is the effect of the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, which multiplies the expected number of visits by a constant factor. The same one-condition increase therefore adds more visits when the expected count is already high than when it is low.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Justifying the choice
I carry the hurdle negative binomial model forward. The DHARMa zero-inflation test showed that the NB2 still produced fewer zeros than observed (observed/expected = 1.1, p = .008), so the zeros needed their own process. The ZINB fit significantly better than the NB2 (χ²(7) = 143.1, p < .001). AIC and BIC agreed that the hurdle model was best of the three: its AIC was 24,330.4 compared with 24,340.8 for the ZINB and 24,469.9 for the NB2, and its BIC was 24,426.3 compared with 24,436.6 and 24,521.0. The hurdle model reproduced the observed zeros (observed/expected = 1, p = 1.000), and the ZINB did so as well (0.96, p = .172), so the choice between them rests on AIC and BIC. The hurdle model also has a natural interpretation for physician visits: one part asks whether a person had any visit at all, and the other asks how many visits they made among those who did. One caution is that the dispersion tests were slightly significant for both zero models (hurdle ratio = 1.15, p = .004), although the ratios are close to 1 and a test on 4,406 observations can flag small departures. I treat this as a minor limitation and not as a reason to prefer the NB2, which cannot reproduce the zeros.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Prediction
I predicted that the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits would be stronger for people with private insurance than for people without it. Private insurance lowers the cost of seeing a doctor, so insured people with more chronic conditions should find it easier to turn their health needs into additional visits, whereas people without private insurance may limit their visits even when they have many conditions. I therefore expected a steeper positive slope of chronic conditions for the insured group.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
text:
Fit the interaction model
The interaction is added to the count part of the hurdle model, so it concerns the number of visits among people who made at least one visit. The zero part keeps all five predictors as additive controls.

title: Count Regression: Poisson, Negative Binomial, and Probing Interactions
section: Test whether the interaction is needed
text:
Test whether the interaction is needed
A likelihood-ratio test comparing the additive hurdle model with the interaction model gave χ²(1) = 0.34, p = .559. The interaction did not significantly improve model fit.
This omnibus test only tells us whether the slope of chronic conditions differs by insurance status. It does not tell us how large the slope is in each group, whether each slope is different from zero, or at what numbers of chronic conditions the groups differ. Probing the interaction answers those questions.

Comparing the two slopes with pairs() gave a difference of 0.016 (SE = 0.028, p = .560). This reproduces the interaction coefficient from the model (-0.016, SE = 0.028, p = .560) with the sign flipped, because pairs() computes the slope for people without insurance minus the slope for people with insurance, whereas the coefficient is the extra slope for people with insurance. The two tests answer the same question when the moderator has only two levels, because the difference between the two slopes is exactly the interaction coefficient. The small difference between the p-value here and the likelihood-ratio p-value above arises because pairs() uses a Wald z-test and the omnibus test is a likelihood-ratio test.
